models.collectorNote: Good cars trade in the millions; SVs are the top of the market. Nearly every Miura has been restored at least once — originality of details is where the money is.

generations.name: Production run
generations.note: The engine was mounted transversely, mid-ship, with the gearbox sharing the sump — compact, clever and a nightmare to service. SV models got wider rear bodywork, more power and, finally, a separated oil supply.

models.intro: The car that invented the mid-engined supercar. Ferruccio Lamborghini's young engineers built it after hours, against his wishes — he wanted a grand tourer. The transverse V12 layout rewrote the rulebook permanently, and Gandini's styling has never been bettered at Sant'Agata.
models.name: Miura

models.collectorNote: Early 'Periscopio' LP400s are the blue-chip cars; Anniversary editions are the most common and the softest-valued. V12 engine-out work is a when, not an if.

generations.name: LP400 / LP400 S
generations.note: The pure original had no rear wing and narrow tyres. The famous optional wing on later cars added drag and nothing else — owners fitted it anyway, because it looked right.

generations.name: LP5000 S / QV
generations.note: Displacement grew to 4.8, then 5.2 litres with four valves per cylinder in the Quattrovalvole — the fastest Countach, at around 455 hp in European tune.

generations.name: 25th Anniversary
generations.note: Restyled under Horacio Pagani, of all people, with heavy visual addenda. The best-selling Countach variant and the one most people picture.

models.intro: The wedge. Gandini's scissor-doored V12 spent sixteen years as the definitive poster car, growing wider, wingier and faster the whole way. Impractical, cramped, nearly impossible to reverse — and completely untouchable as an object.
models.name: Countach

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: All-wheel drive and a dual-clutch gearbox made it the first junior Lamborghini that was genuinely easy to drive fast. The rear-drive LP 580-2 followed for people who wanted the old edge back.

generations.name: Huracán Evo and derivatives
generations.note: More power, rear-wheel steering and a central computer predicting grip before you need it. The run ended with specials like the track-focused STO and the off-road Sterrato.

models.intro: The Gallardo's successor and the last of the naturally aspirated V10s. Over two decades of production variants — Evo, Performante, STO, Tecnica, Sterrato — made it Lamborghini's best-selling sports car before the Temerario replaced it in 2024.
models.name: Huracán

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: A new carbon monocoque and a single-clutch ISR gearbox that shifted brutally fast — and felt it. The SV of 2015 sharpened everything and lapped the Nürburgring in under seven minutes.

generations.name: Second phase
generations.note: The S added rear-wheel steering and 740 PS. The SVJ took the Nürburgring production record in 2018; the Ultimae, limited to 600 cars, closed the non-hybrid V12 era.

models.intro: The V12 flagship for a decade: carbon monocoque, pushrod suspension, scissor doors, and a 6.5-litre V12 that outlived three generations of rivals. Replaced by the hybrid Revuelto, which makes the Aventador the last pure-V12 Lamborghini flagship.
models.name: Aventador

generations.name: Urus
generations.note: Built on the same platform as the Audi Q8 and Bentley Bentayga, but tuned with real aggression. The Performante dropped weight and added a Rally mode; it promptly set a Pikes Peak SUV record.

generations.name: Urus SE
generations.note: Plug-in hybrid: the V8 plus an electric motor for 789 hp combined and a usable electric range. Now the default Urus, whether the purists like it or not.

models.intro: The 'Super SUV' that doubled Lamborghini's sales and paid for everything else in the catalogue. Purists scoffed in 2018; the order books answered. Genuinely fast, genuinely usable, and the reason Lamborghini can still afford V12 flagships.
models.name: Urus
